title: Armuth und Demuth führen zum Himmel
titleEn: Poverty and Humility Lead to Heaven
part: Poverty and Humility Lead to Heaven
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 204. Text from Wikisource („Armuth und Demuth führen zum Himmel (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: The title states its own moral: poverty and humility lead to heaven. On an old beggar's advice, a king's son trades his fine clothes for rags and wanders seven years in want; back home and unrecognized, fed in secret under the palace stairs, he dies holding a rose in one hand and a lily in the other, and both flowers grow from his grave.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Königssohn, der gieng hinaus in das Feld und war nachdenklich und traurig.
sentences.l: There was once a king’s son, who went out into the field and was pensive and sad.
sentences.n: “gieng” = ging (1857 spelling). “hinaus” — separable, “out”; the direction is away from where he was. “nachdenklich” — thoughtful, meditative; a plain word, not brooding or troubled.

sentences.t: Er sah den Himmel an, der war so schön rein und blau, da seufzte er und sprach „wie wohl muß einem erst da oben im Himmel sein!“
sentences.l: He looked up at the sky, which was so beautifully clear and blue; then he sighed and said, “How well one must feel first of all up there in heaven!”
sentences.i: He looked up at the sky, which was so beautifully clear and blue, and sighed and said, “How well one must feel up there in heaven!”
sentences.n: “ansehen” — to look at (separable an-, here in the past “sah … an”). “Himmel” carries both senses at once — sky (that he sees) and heaven (that he longs for); the same word will now be used throughout in both senses. “einem … wohl sein” — impersonal dative, “to feel well” (literally, “to one it must be so well”). “erst” here is an intensifier — “only just imagine,” “truly, how well.”

sentences.t: Da erblickte er einen armen greisen Mann, der des Weges daher kam, redete ihn an und fragte „wie kann ich wohl in den Himmel kommen?“
sentences.l: Then he caught sight of a poor aged man who was coming along the way, addressed him, and asked, “How can I get into heaven?”
sentences.i: Then he caught sight of a poor old man coming along the road, called out to him and asked, “How can I get into heaven?”
sentences.n: “greis” — venerable and grey with age; “ein greiser Mann” is a stock formula. “des Weges” — genitive of place, “along the way,” an elevated turn. “anreden” — to address, to speak to (separable an-).

sentences.t: Der Mann antwortete „durch Armuth und Demuth.
sentences.l: The man answered, “Through poverty and humility.
sentences.n: The title-phrase of the legend, spoken now in reply. “Armuth” and “Demuth” are 1857 spellings of Armut and Demut. “Demuth” is the plain Christian virtue — humility, the disposition of one who bows before God — not any grander mystical meaning.

sentences.t: Leg an meine zerrissenen Kleider, wandere sieben Jahre in der Welt und lerne ihr Elend kennen: nimm kein Geld, sondern wenn du hungerst, bitt mitleidige Herzen um ein Stückchen Brot, so wirst du dich dem Himmel nähern.“
sentences.l: Put on my ragged clothes, wander seven years in the world and learn to know its misery; take no money, but when you hunger, beg pitying hearts for a little piece of bread, so shall you draw near to heaven.”
sentences.i: Put on my ragged clothes, wander seven years about the world and come to know its misery; take no money, but when you go hungry, beg pitying hearts for a little piece of bread — so will you draw near to heaven.”
sentences.n: “anlegen” — to put on (clothes); separable an-. “kennen lernen” — to come to know, to get to know; here in an infinitive construction. “bitt” is an unusual short imperative of bitten (normally bitte); Grimm preserves it. “sich dem Himmel nähern” — nähern takes the dative, “to draw near to heaven.” Note also the plain, unmystical “Himmel” — the same word he saw in the sky above.

sentences.t: Da zog der Königssohn seinen prächtigen Rock aus und hieng dafür das Bettlergewand um, gieng hinaus in die weite Welt und duldete groß Elend.
sentences.l: Then the king’s son drew off his splendid coat and hung the beggar’s garment around himself instead, went out into the wide world and endured great misery.
sentences.i: Then the king’s son took off his splendid coat and put on the beggar’s garment instead, went out into the wide world, and endured great misery.
sentences.n: “ausziehen” and “umhängen” are both separable — “zog … aus,” “hieng … um”; the particles come at the end of their clauses. “Bettlergewand” — beggar’s garment (Bettler + Gewand). “groß Elend” — the adjective is uninflected, an older poetic usage, for “great misery.”

sentences.t: Er nahm nichts als ein wenig Essen, sprach nichts, sondern betete zu dem Herrn daß er ihn einmal in seinen Himmel aufnehmen wollte.
sentences.l: He took nothing but a little food, said nothing, but prayed to the Lord that he would take him one day into his heaven.
sentences.i: He took nothing but a little food, said nothing, but prayed to the Lord that he would one day take him up into his heaven.
sentences.n: “nichts als” — nothing but, only. “sondern” contrasts against a preceding negation (nichts): “not … but rather.” “einmal” here = “one day, at some point,” not “once.” “aufnehmen” — to take up, to receive (separable auf-).

sentences.t: Als die sieben Jahre herum waren, da kam er wieder an seines Vaters Schloß, aber niemand erkannte ihn.
sentences.l: When the seven years were round, he came again to his father’s castle, but no one knew him.
sentences.i: When the seven years were up, he came back to his father’s castle, but no one recognised him.
sentences.n: “herum sein” — to be round, i.e. to be over, past (of a stretch of time). “seines Vaters Schloß” — genitive before the noun, a formal older word order (modern: das Schloß seines Vaters). “erkennen” — to recognise (someone).

sentences.t: Er sprach zu den Dienern „geht und sagt meinen Eltern daß ich wiedergekommen bin.“
sentences.l: He said to the servants, “Go and tell my parents that I have come back.”
sentences.n: Notice the reversed order of address: he is a king’s son giving an order to the servants of his own house. “wiedergekommen” — perfect of wiederkommen (separable wieder-). The daß-clause here follows sagen and carries the reported content.

sentences.t: Aber die Diener glaubten es nicht, lachten und ließen ihn stehen.
sentences.l: But the servants did not believe it, laughed, and left him standing there.
sentences.n: “jemanden stehen lassen” — literally, to leave someone standing; the idiom is “to walk away from someone,” to leave without response. A cold refusal.

sentences.t: Da sprach er „geht und sagts meinen Brüdern, daß sie herab kommen, ich möchte sie so gerne wieder sehen.“
sentences.l: Then he said, “Go and say it to my brothers, that they should come down, I would so gladly see them again.”
sentences.i: Then he said, “Go and tell my brothers to come down; I would so love to see them again.”
sentences.n: “sagts” = sagt es — the enclitic ’s for es, common in colloquial German and preserved by Grimm. “möchte” + gerne — a soft, longing wish: “I would so gladly …” “herab kommen” — separable, “to come down.” The daß-clause here reads as an indirect command (that they should come).

sentences.t: Sie wollten auch nicht, bis endlich einer von ihnen hingieng und es den Königskindern sagte, aber diese glaubten es nicht und bekümmerten sich nicht darum.
sentences.l: They too did not want to, until at last one of them went thither and said it to the king’s children, but these did not believe it and did not concern themselves about it.
sentences.i: They too refused, until at last one of them went and told the king’s children, but they did not believe it either, and gave it no thought.
sentences.n: “hingieng” — separable “hingehen,” to go thither (1857 gieng). “die Königskinder” — the king’s children, i.e. the beggar’s own royal brothers and sisters. “sich bekümmern um” — to concern oneself about, to be troubled about.

sentences.t: Da schrieb er einen Brief an seine Mutter, und beschrieb ihr darin all sein Elend, aber er sagte nicht daß er ihr Sohn wäre.
sentences.l: Then he wrote a letter to his mother, and described to her therein all his misery, but he did not say that he was her son.
sentences.i: Then he wrote a letter to his mother, and set out for her in it all his misery, but he did not say that he was her son.
sentences.n: “darin” — therein, in it (referring to the letter). “wäre” — past subjunctive of sein in reported speech, showing that his self-identification is what he holds back.

sentences.t: Da ließ ihm die Königin aus Mitleid einen Platz unter der Treppe anweisen und ihm täglich durch zwei Diener Essen bringen.
sentences.l: Then the queen, out of pity, had a place assigned to him beneath the stair, and had food brought to him daily by two servants.
sentences.i: Then the queen, out of pity, had a place assigned to him under the stair and had food brought to him daily by two servants.
sentences.n: “ließ … anweisen” and “ließ … bringen” — a causative lassen construction: “had (someone) do (something).” “aus Mitleid” — out of pity. The mother houses her own son under the stairs without knowing him.

sentences.t: Aber der eine war bös und sprach „was soll dem Bettler das gute Essen!“ behielts für sich oder gabs den Hunden und brachte dem Schwachen, Abgezehrten nur Wasser;
sentences.l: But the one was wicked and said, “What is the good food for the beggar!” — kept it for himself or gave it to the dogs, and brought only water to the weak, wasted man;
sentences.i: But the one was wicked and said, “What good is fine food to a beggar!” — kept it for himself or gave it to the dogs, and brought only water to the weakened, wasted man;
sentences.n: “behielts” = behielt es; “gabs” = gab es — the ’s enclitic again. “dem Bettler … das Essen” — dative of the person, “what is the food for the beggar,” an idiomatic construction of value or purpose. “der Abgezehrte” — the wasted, emaciated one; from abzehren (to eat away, to waste).

sentences.t: doch der andere war ehrlich und brachte ihm was er für ihn bekam.
sentences.l: but the other was honest and brought him what he received for him.
sentences.n: “bekam” here is 3rd sg. past of bekommen — to receive, get (a common false friend of English “become”).

sentences.t: Es war wenig, doch konnte er davon eine Zeit lang leben; dabei war er ganz geduldig, bis er immer schwächer ward.
sentences.l: It was little, yet he could live from it for a time; and with it he was quite patient, until he grew ever weaker.
sentences.i: It was little, yet he could live on it for a time; through it all he was quite patient, until he grew ever weaker.
sentences.n: “davon leben” — to live on it, to subsist from it. “dabei” here = at the same time, through it all. “ward” = wurde (older past of werden). The devotional register here is plain: patience unto weakening, not any staged suffering.

sentences.t: Als aber seine Krankheit zunahm, da begehrte er das heil. Abendmahl zu empfangen.
sentences.l: But as his sickness increased, he desired to receive the holy Communion.
sentences.n: “zunahm” — separable “zunehmen,” to increase (of a state, an illness, a weight). “heil.” is the abbreviation for “heilig” (holy) — printed abbreviated in 1857. “das Abendmahl” — the Lord’s Supper, Holy Communion; literally “evening meal,” but by the Reformation the settled German word for the Eucharist.

sentences.t: Wie es nun unter der halben Messe ist, fangen von selbst alle Glocken in der Stadt und in der Gegend an zu läuten.
sentences.l: As it now is under the middle of the Mass, all the bells in the town and in the region begin of themselves to ring.
sentences.i: As it happens now, in the middle of the Mass, all the bells in the town and the region begin of themselves to ring.
sentences.n: “wie es ist” — “as it is [that],” a narrative turn: “now it happens that …” “unter der halben Messe” — under, i.e. during, the halfway point of the Mass. “von selbst” — of itself, by itself, without human doing — the miraculous note. “fangen … an zu” — separable anfangen zu + infinitive, to begin to.

sentences.t: Der Geistliche geht nach der Messe zu dem armen Mann unter der Treppe, so liegt er da todt, in der einen Hand eine Rose, in der andern eine Lilie, und neben ihm ein Papier, darauf steht seine Geschichte aufgeschrieben.
sentences.l: The clergyman goes after the Mass to the poor man beneath the stair, and so there he lies dead, in the one hand a rose, in the other a lily, and beside him a paper, on which stands his story written down.
sentences.i: After the Mass, the clergyman goes to the poor man under the stair, and there he lies dead, in one hand a rose, in the other a lily, and beside him a paper on which his story stands written down.
sentences.n: The tense shifts to the historical present at the moment of discovery — “geht … liegt … steht.” “Geistliche” — clergyman, priest (substantival adjective). “darauf steht … aufgeschrieben” — “on which stands written down”; “aufgeschrieben” is the past participle of aufschreiben (to write down, separable auf-). Rose and lily are traditional emblems of martyrdom and purity in Christian iconography; the paper simply reports what the tale has just shown.

sentences.t: Als er begraben war, wuchs auf der einen Seite des Grabes eine Rose, auf der andern eine Lilie heraus.
sentences.l: When he had been buried, there grew out on one side of the grave a rose, on the other a lily.
sentences.i: When he had been buried, a rose grew out on one side of the grave, and a lily on the other.
sentences.n: “begraben” — past participle of begraben (to bury); “als er begraben war” = when he had been buried, past passive. “heraus wachsen” is separable — “wuchs … heraus,” “to grow out.” The single-sentence closing block, set off in the 1857 printing, seals the miracle: the emblems in his dead hands rise again from the grave.

glossary.bitt: bitten — beg, ask (imperative sg.; Grimm's short form of modern bitte)
glossary.gabs: gab es — gave it (gab + clitic es; 'gabs den Hunden' = gave it to the dogs)
glossary.heil: heilig — holy (here the abbreviation 'heil.' for heiliges; 'das heil. Abendmahl' = the holy Communion)
glossary.leben: leben — to live (infinitive; 'davon leben' = to live on it)
glossary.leg: legen — lay, put (imperative sg.; here anlegen, to put on, with 'an' at the end)
glossary.ließen: lassen — let, allowed (3rd pl. past; 'ließen ihn stehen' = left him standing)
glossary.messe: die Messe — the Mass, the church service (here 'unter der halben Messe' = during the middle of the Mass; the same word also = trade fair)
glossary.sagt: sagen — tell, say (imperative pl.; 'geht und sagt' = go and tell)
glossary.sagts: sagt es — tell it (imperative pl. + clitic es; 'geht und sagts' = go and tell it)
